blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome to our fiftieth episode of Michael's Morning Listening!
Today we first look back at ten of our favourite stories from the past fifty episodes.
Then we follow a tiny traveller — a sound — all the way into your ear.
Ready?
Let's go!
Do you remember the flying car?
It drove on the road like a car, then spread its wings and flew into the sky!
And the bees that learned to play football — they pushed the ball into the goal, one tiny kick at a time.
Messi said goodbye to Argentina's home stadium, and the fans sang his name.
A robot ran a half marathon beside human runners — slow, steady, and never giving up.
A pumpkin grew heavier than a rhino, so big that a whole family could sit inside it!
A cat became the boss of a library, sleeping on the books and greeting every reader at the door.
A hundred-year-old grandpa jumped out of a plane with a parachute — age is only a number!
A penguin proposed with a pebble, offering the smoothest stone he could find to the one he loved.
The mantis shrimp sees colours we cannot imagine, with eyes that move on their own.
And Lucy, the little girl who grew a sunflower taller than a bus — small hands, huge surprise!
Every sound begins with a shake.
Hit a drum, and its skin shakes back and forth.
That shake is called a vibration, and it pushes the air into a wave.
Our approach is simple: follow that wave, step by step, all the way into your ear.
First, your outer ear catches the wave and funnels it down the ear canal to a thin piece of tissue called the eardrum.
The wave makes the eardrum shake!
Next, the shake reaches three tiny bones — the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup.
They are the smallest bones in your body, and they conduct the shake onward, making it stronger.
Then comes the most amazing aspect: a snail-shaped room full of fluid, called the cochlea.
Inside, thousands of tiny hair cells bend like grass in the wind, and their bending turns the shake into electrical signals.
Those signals race along the auditory nerve to your brain, and your brain reads them as a sparrow's song, a friend's laugh, or music.
Sound moves as a pulse through the air at about 343 metres every second.
And here is a fun fact: sound needs something to travel through.
In empty space, with no air at all, there is no sound — that is why space is silent!
So remember the journey: shake, wave, eardrum, bones, cochlea, brain — all in less than a blink!
Today's idiom is "your guess is as good as mine." It means "I don't know either!" For example: if you ask me how many songs a sparrow can sing, your guess is as good as mine!
Try it: when a friend asks you something nobody knows, just smile and say: your guess is as good as mine!
Now it is your turn!
One: which of our ten favourite stories do you like best, and why?
Two: sound cannot travel in empty space — can you think of another place where sound travels, like water or a wall?
Talk about it with your family!
That is all for today, young explorers — and thank you for fifty wonderful episodes!
Keep your ears open, keep asking questions, and we will meet tomorrow morning.
Goodbye, and have a wonderful day!
